subject: big differences between brms and rstanarm

messages.author: 0d4085b4474fa32a
messages.subject: big differences between brms and rstanarm
parts:
I'm seeing some strange differences in the population level effects between brms and rstanarm. I'm attaching the dataset.

I'm using quite weak priors, so I wouldn't expect them to change my posterior so much. I think that the posteriors of rstanarm make more sense, so I might be doing something wrong with brms.

This is the output of brms:

df_F05 <- read.table("Data/Fuchs_2005_complete.tsv", sep="\t", header=T)
df_F05 %<>% mutate(cvoicing=if_else(voicing=="voiced",.5,-.5))

head(df_F05)

#   publication subject experiment    dur voicing stimuli pair cvoicing
# 1  Fuchs_2005      cg        ema 189.87  voiced  gedaad   aa      0.5
# 2  Fuchs_2005      cg        ema 178.56  voiced  gedaad   aa      0.5
# 3  Fuchs_2005      cg        ema 184.19  voiced  gedaad   aa      0.5
# 4  Fuchs_2005      cg        ema 177.50  voiced  gedaad   aa      0.5
# 5  Fuchs_2005      cg        ema 200.31  voiced  gedaad   aa      0.5
# 6  Fuchs_2005      cg        ema 184.56  voiced  gedaad   aa      0.5


quantile(df_F05$dur, c(.275,.5,.975))
 #  27.5%     50%   97.5%
 # 91.000 113.895 193.000

# Linear mixed model:
fit_F05 <- brm(dur ~  cvoicing + (cvoicing|pair)  +(cvoicing|subject), data = df_F05,
    prior= c(prior(normal(0,300), class = Intercept),
             prior(normal(0,100), class = b, coef = cvoicing),
             prior(normal(0,100), class = sd),
             prior(normal(0,100), class = sigma),
             prior(lkj(2), class = cor)
             ),iter=iter,
                control=list(adapt_delta=.9999, max_treedepth=17))


fit_F05
#  Family: gaussian
#   Links: mu = identity; sigma = identity
# Formula: dur ~ cvoicing + (cvoicing | pair) + (cvoicing | subject)
#    Data: df_F05 (Number of observations: 270)
# Samples: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
#          total post-warmup samples = 4000
#     ICs: LOO = NA; WAIC = NA; R2 = NA
 
# Group-Level Effects:
# ~pair (Number of levels: 3)
#                         Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
# sd(Intercept)              57.74     35.21    18.68   153.36       1779 1.00
# sd(cvoicing)               10.60     17.17     0.22    59.60       1003 1.01
# cor(Intercept,cvoicing)     0.05      0.45    -0.78     0.84       4000 1.00

# ~subject (Number of levels: 3)
#                         Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
# sd(Intercept)              49.39     33.75    14.23   140.22       1808 1.00
# sd(cvoicing)               19.95     22.81     1.95    88.47       1119 1.00
# cor(Intercept,cvoicing)    -0.02      0.45    -0.82     0.78       3324 1.00

# Population-Level Effects:
#           Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
# Intercept   115.71     49.18    19.63   221.39       1178 1.01
# cvoicing     31.83     20.78   -16.44    69.75       1294 1.00

# Family Specific Parameters:
#       Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Eff.Sample Rhat
# sigma    14.54      0.63    13.38    15.83       4000 1.00

# Samples were drawn using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Eff.Sample
# is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential
# scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).


I think that the population level-effects are too wide. Given the quantiles of the variable dur (above), the posterior of the Intercept seems unreasonable. And I also think that the posterior of cvoicing is too wide.


If I try rstanarm these posteriors make more sense (to me). I know the models aren't exactly the same (because of the centered intercept), but I wouldn't expect such a big difference:


fit_F05s <- stan_glmer(dur ~  cvoicing  + (cvoicing|pair)+(cvoicing|subject), data = df_F05, prior = normal(0,100), prior_intercept = normal(0,300),  prior_aux = normal(0,100),prior_covariance=decov(2), adapt_delta=.9999, family = gaussian(),iter=iter)

messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Re: big differences between brms and rstanarm
parts:
I wouldn't call those "big" differences ;-)

They are driven by rstanarm's default priors, which can end up being rather informative for small data sets.

See also https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/brms-users/gj5-NvAUlEU

By the way, this dataset is quite small, with similar models but more data, I  only see minor differences between rstanarm and brms.

parts:
I wouldn't call those "big" differences ;-)

They are driven by rstanarm's default priors, which can end up being rather informative for small data sets.

See also https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/brms-users/gj5-NvAUlEU

By the way, this dataset is quite small, with similar models but more data, I  only see minor differences between rstanarm and brms.
